Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

each adjective and pronoun

also each one, each of them, each in his own place, one each, all the best, all the wisest

classical

Cato Agr. 5.5: utī suō quisque locō cubet
Cic. Amic. 62: quot quisque habēret
Traupman 308

quisque, quaeque, quodque

pronoun and adjective (as a pronoun, neuter quicque); never first in its clause

each, each one

The “each” of more than two; of two, uterque (see both). It leans on the word before it: after sē or suus (suō quisque locō, each in his own place), after a relative or a question word (quot quisque habēret, how many each had), after a superlative or an ordinal (see every). With a superlative, “all the …, every one in his degree”: sapientissimus quisque, all the wisest; neuter optimum quidque, all the best things.

Other words

  • ūnusquisque, ūnaquaeque, ūnumquodque — each single one, every one

    pronoun and adjective; both parts decline (dat. ūnīcuique); also written apart · also used · classical · Cato Agr. 58: salis ūnīcuique in annō modium satis est

  • singulī, singulae, singula — each one separately; one to each

    distributive adjective, plural, declension · also used · classical · Tac. Germ. 22.1: sēparātae singulīs sēdēs; Cato Agr. 148.1: in culleōs singulōs (Lewis & Short)

    Each by himself, one apiece; opposed to ūniversī, all together. With a distributive number, so many each: bīnī, two each (see two each).

Examples

  • prius vīllam videat clausa utī siet, et utī suō quisque locō cubet

    first let him see that the farmhouse is locked, and that each man is sleeping in his own placeCato Agr. 5.5

  • haec postquam omnia sēcrēvimus, tum suō quaeque locō disposuimus

    when we had sorted all these things, we put each in its own placeCol. 12.3.3

  • lautī cibum capiunt: sēparātae singulīs sēdēs et sua cuique mēnsa

    when they have washed, they eat: each has a seat of his own and his own tableTac. Germ. 22.1

  • ut quisque aetāte antecēdit, ita sententiae prīncipātum tenet

    each speaks first as he is first in ageCic. Sen. 64

  • salis ūnīcuique in annō modium satis est

    a peck of salt a year is enough for each manCato Agr. 58

  • sapientissimus quisque aequissimō animō moritur, stultissimus inīquissimō

    the wisest die with the calmest mind, the most foolish with the least calmCic. Sen. 83

  • in omnī enim arte vel studiō vel quāvīs scientiā vel in ipsā virtūte optimum quidque rārissimum est

    for in every art or study or any knowledge, or in virtue itself, the best is always the rarestCic. Fin. 2.81

See also every, all, everyone, two each, both, one of.
